Nine-67Open demo in presenter mode ↗
Suuchi Ramesh + Josh Lee · Friday, November 6 · 1:00–1:30 PM ET

Host guide

Your team has AI. Why is the work still manual?

Present at the plain address (cover → opening stats → seven-screen demo). Attendees see no presenter buttons. Rehearse by opening any page once with ?presenter=1: that tab then shows Mode, Host guide, notes and Presenter resources. Use ?presenter=0 to switch it off. Keep this guide on a second screen, never on the shared one. Arrow keys move forward and back on every page.

Core line: “AI made each person faster. Nobody redesigned the handoffs between them.”

Name the gap in four minutes

1:00:00 · Hook “Raise your hand, or type yes, if your team has ChatGPT or Copilot. Now keep it up if a request still gets copied between three tools before it’s done.”

Poll 1 (launch now): “Where does AI live in your company today?” (a) Individual chat tools (b) A few team workflows (c) Embedded in cross-team processes (d) Not sure

1:00:45 · Disclosure and CTA touch #1 “Everything you’ll see is a fictional company and a working simulation of a pattern we build. At the end we’ll offer a small number of complimentary workflow assessments, so keep one handoff in mind as we go.”

Josh posts the booking link in chat and the resource panel now. Booking link needed

1:01:30 · Evidence Josh advances to the stats screen. Suuchi: “McKinsey’s State of AI this year: 80% say AI made them more productive, but only 37% see any impact on EBIT, the same as last year. Atlassian found 85% use AI at work, but only 29% have built it into how work actually flows. And Miro, just this week: 69% say most AI work happens in private sessions. Faster people. Same company.” Josh: “That’s what we’ll show you.”

Read the Poll 1 result aloud. Then: “AI made each person faster. Nobody redesigned the handoffs between them. Josh, show us one.”

1:04:00–1:11:30 · Josh shares, Suuchi asks

One order, two logos, one decision: can the operator hit Start?

1:04:00 · Set up (30 seconds). “We’re going to follow one customer order through a company that has AI in every department. Watch one thing: what goes on the shirt.” Then go to screen 1.

  1. 1:04:30–1:05:15 · Screen 1 · The order

    One order, two logos

    Josh “Meet Keystone Workwear. They print uniforms for national service companies. Monday, 8:41, their customer Ridgeline Roofing emails: we approved the new logo this morning, use it on all 5,000 shirts, are we still good for Friday?”

    Josh “Leah, the account manager, has Copilot draft the reply: got it, we’ll use the new logo. Look at both logos. Remember the new one.”

    Point to the email, the reply, then the two shirts. Suuchi asks “When a customer changes an order in your company, where does that change actually land?”

  2. 1:05:15–1:06:00 · Screen 2 · Three AIs

    Your AI rollout worked

    Josh “This is the company that did everything right. Leah used Copilot to answer the customer. Dana used an AI tool to check the new file. Sam used a scheduling copilot to move the job up and protect Friday. Three good AI outputs.”

    Read the red line on each card as it appears: the file stays in the email thread, the work order still points to the old file, the press prints whatever is marked Approved. Then the callout: “Nobody changed the order.” Mention the “Private session” tags: “Miro found that’s where 69% of AI work happens.”

  3. 1:06:00–1:07:00 · Screen 3 · The press

    The moment: would you hit Start?

    Josh “This is the press operator’s screen at 12:58. Order 4821, 5,000 shirts, artwork approved. Knowing what this operator knows, would you hit Start?”

    Ask it and wait. The “Old logo” stamp lands after three seconds; let it. Then point at the three boxes on the right: the new logo is in Leah’s email and on the shared drive, but the work order still points to the old file. Suuchi: “Nobody did anything wrong. The rep treated a reply as a change. Design treated saving a file as a handoff. Production trusted the approved work order.”

  4. 1:07:00–1:08:15 · Screen 4 · The fallout

    The fear

    Josh “1:00 PM, the press starts. By 5:20, all 5,000 are printed and boxed, ahead of schedule. Friday morning, the Denver branch opens a box: these have our old logo. Friday afternoon, Rachel writes: we relaunch at 40 branches Monday. You confirmed the change. Every AI did its job. The company still broke a promise.”

    Read the four messages as they appear. The clock jumps from Monday to Friday and turns red. Pause on “You confirmed the change.” Suuchi asks “How many of these are in flight in your company right now?” Then the Real data box: “Workday found nearly 40% of the time AI saves is lost to rework.” Close on the bottom line: it’s every handoff between two people’s AI.

  5. 1:08:15–1:10:00 · Screen 5 · The desk

    The fix: same email, fixed before the press

    Josh “Back to Monday, 8:47. Same email. This time it doesn’t stop at a reply. The desk matches it to order 4821 and shows Leah the one fact that matters: 5,000 shirts print at 1:00 today, with the old logo. Leah holds the job. Dana approves the new proof against this order, not just a file on a drive. Now production can release it.”

    Josh “And this isn’t bot number 41. 84% of CIOs say people are building agents faster than IT can govern them. This is one agent that connects the email, the file and the work order, then waits for a person.”

    Let the rewind play (about two seconds, the date spins back from Friday to Monday) before you speak. The clock ticks 8:47 to 8:52 as the log fills, then the proposal appears. Click Release with new artwork. Say: “Nothing prints until a person approves.” Leave Change one fact for Q&A.

  6. 1:10:00–1:11:00 · Screen 6 · Right shirt

    Watch the logo change

    Josh “Back to the operator’s screen. Watch the logo change. Same press, same 1:00 slot, Friday holds. And only now does Leah confirm with the customer.”

    Josh, slowly “The customer asked us to change what went on the shirt. We used AI to answer the email, check the artwork, and schedule the press. Who changed what went on the shirt?”

    Say “In this demo the work order update is simulated. In a real build we use your ERP’s API.” Point to the before and after: found at the branches versus fixed by 8:55.

1:11:00 Leave screen 6 up for the debrief.

Suuchi “One change, three departments, one hold, done. Where in your business does a customer change stop at a reply? Type it in chat.”

Josh “The desk connects the change to the order, attaches the facts, and routes one decision to its owner. That before and after is exactly what we measure in an assessment: handoffs, wait time, approver, and one baseline metric.”

Map one attendee workflow, then Q&A

1:19–1:24 · Attendee case. Take one chat answer and map its handoffs out loud: who asks, who checks, which systems, who approves, who waits.

1:24–1:27:30 · Q&A. Use the answers below. To show the desk holds instead of guessing, open screen 5 with Change one fact:

  • Proof approved. Release is available.
  • Proof not approved yet. The headline becomes “Hold: waiting on the proof.” Nothing prints until design approves.
  • File fails the print check. The headline becomes “Hold: the new file can’t print.” Leah asks the customer for a vector file before anyone confirms Friday.
1:27:30–1:30:00 · Suuchi · Screen 7

“Here’s the assessment. It’s 45 minutes with Josh and me. You leave with a one-page map of one workflow: every handoff, the wait time, the approver, and where AI can complete the step versus assist. No system access, no obligation, not a sales pitch. We run these ourselves, so we’re holding [N] sessions in November. Use the link, scan the code, type ‘assessment’ in chat, or reply to the follow-up email. Thanks for spending your Friday with us.”

Optional last line, Josh “The customer asked us to change what went on the shirt. Who in your company changes what goes on the shirt?”

End at 1:30. Even if the demo failed, do this close.

Within 24 hours: send the replay and booking link to all registrants. Send a personal note to everyone who typed a workflow, quoting it back. Prioritize Poll 1 answer (a).

Q&A answers

“Won’t Microsoft or Salesforce fix this?”
“Every vendor now names the silo problem and sells its own platform as the one hub. Buy three and you have three hubs. A registry tells you an agent exists. It doesn’t read two managers’ plans and fix the conflict. We connect the AI you already pay for to the systems you already own.”
“Isn’t this just vendor hype?”
“The independent data says the same thing. McKinsey: 80% feel more productive, 37% see it in EBIT. PwC: 56% of CEOs say AI hasn’t delivered significant financial benefit yet. The UK government’s own Copilot trial found no robust evidence that time savings improved productivity.”
“We tried agents and they failed.”
“Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by 2027, for cost, unclear value or weak risk controls. That’s why we scope to one painful handoff, with a human approval and an audit trail, and measure it in weeks.”
“How do we show ROI to the board?”
“Don’t count seats or agents. Count handoffs removed, wait time cut, and escalations avoided in one workflow. That’s what the assessment baselines.”
“We already have dozens of bots. Isn’t this one more?”
“84% of CIOs say people build agents faster than IT can govern them. This isn’t bot number 41. It’s one agent that reads across the work the others produce, writes back to your system of record, and waits for a named person to approve.”
“We already pay for Copilot. Why do we need this?”
“Keep it. In the demo, Copilot did its job: it wrote Leah a good reply. The delay is the handoff between people and systems. That’s the layer we build, using the tools you already own.”
“How do we trust it not to hallucinate?”
“We never design for blind trust. Every step pulls from your system of record, shows its sources, and stops for a person on anything consequential. Trust in fully autonomous agents fell from 43% to 27% in a year, per Capgemini. That’s why we build supervised workflows.”
“Where’s the human? Who approves?”
“You decide per step. Reversible, low-risk steps run on their own. Money, customer and people decisions stop for a named approver. You saw it: nothing printed until production released it, and when the proof wasn’t approved, the desk held.”
“What data does it touch? Is it secure?”
“Only what that workflow needs, with its own scoped credentials, inside your tenant, and every action is logged.”
“Our systems are old. Is this a platform overhaul?”
“No. We use APIs where they exist and exports where they don’t, like the work order in the demo. The assessment picks a workflow that touches only a few systems.”
“Was any of that real?”
“The company and data are fictional, and the screens are a working simulation of a pattern we build. In a real engagement the export becomes a tested API connection. We’d rather show you exactly what’s simulated than oversell it.”
“How do we measure ROI?”
“On the workflow, not the chat. Before we build, we baseline cycle time from request to done, handoffs, rework, and cost per completed request, then measure the same numbers after.”
“What does it cost?”
“Build and change management usually cost more than model usage. We set a usage budget per workflow from day one, and the assessment is free and scoped to one workflow.” Agree a pilot price range before Friday
“Won’t this scare our people or cut jobs?”
“We start with the work people dislike: copying, chasing, re-keying. The people who do it today become the approvers and owners. In the demo, Dana still approves the proof. She just stops chasing.”
“Aren’t most AI projects failing?”
“Many are. Gartner predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, because of cost, unclear value or weak controls. The assessment addresses all three up front.”
“Are we locked into a vendor?”
“No. The prompts, rules, evaluations and logs are yours, and the design is model-agnostic.”
“Who’s accountable when it gets it wrong?”
“The same owner who’s accountable for that process today. Every action is logged, and high-impact steps need a named approver.”
“How long until something is live?”
“Assessment first, to map one workflow. Then a scoped build with your process owner and one IT contact.” Agree a concrete timeline before Friday
“This only works for manufacturers, right?”
“Swap the logo for any customer change: a roof spec, a service window, a contract term, a payment date. The change lands in one inbox, and the work runs from somewhere else.”

Do not use: MIT’s “95% of AI pilots fail” (preliminary, publicly critiqued), any McKinsey redesign percentage you haven’t confirmed in the PDF, “Harvard research” for workslop (it was BetterUp and Stanford), or Pamarco and Esker as AI proof. Also: “the only thing worse than not having a copilot is having more than one” (Microsoft’s Judson Althoff, about Microsoft’s own product names, not customers), Workday “37%” (it’s “nearly 40%”), “Deloitte said it has a human intelligence problem” (a senator said it), “shadow AI is in 1 in 5 breaches” (it’s 1 in 5 organizations), and any Reddit, Hacker News or anonymous CIO anecdote as data.

Before going live

  • Fill in dist/site.js: booking link, November slot count, portrait files. The assessment screen and cover update automatically.
  • Rehearse twice in the real webinar platform at 1280×720, including both polls and posting the link in chat.
  • Present from the plain address with no ?presenter=1. Confirm no Mode, Host guide, Reset or notes buttons are visible.
  • Share one browser window in full screen. Bookmarks bar hidden. Do Not Disturb on. Slack, Teams and mail closed on both machines.
  • Run a local copy too (npm run dev, then http://localhost:3000/) in case the network or host fails.
  • Record an 8-minute fallback video of the full flow and keep it open on Josh’s machine.
  • Suuchi has the URL and has clicked through once, in case Josh’s connection drops.
  • Never say “fully autonomous”.

If the shared screen freezes, say: “The customer changed the logo. Leah said got it, design saved the file, production scheduled the press, and the operator would have printed 5,000 shirts with the old logo. The desk connected the email to the order, Leah held it, design approved the proof, and the press still ran at 1:00 with the right shirt.” Don’t retry on stage. Move on to the close.
